tldr: By combining step-to-step prediction using a reduced-order model (ALIP) with discrete exponential control barrier functions (DECBF), this paper proposes a framework for training-time penalty shaping and runtime action filtering in RL-based bipedal locomotion, effectively preventing leg-crossing and falls under external disturbances.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed framework. During training (top), the ALIP model predicts the next pre-impact state from candidate foot placements chosen by the policy, penalizing unsafe states via reward shaping. At runtime (bottom), the same conditions act as a projection filter, minimally adjusting foot placements in real time to remain within the safe set.
overview:
For humanoid robots to operate alongside humans, ensuring safety by preventing falls and self-collisions (such as leg crossing) is critical. Modern reinforcement learning (RL) adapts remarkably well to complex environments, but its black-box nature makes it difficult to mathematically constrain the robot's state at the next impact. Conversely, classical gait generators grounded in reduced-order dynamics offer clear interpretability and predictability, yet they often lack the robustness of RL against disturbances.

To capture the best of both worlds, the authors developed a hybrid approach. Using the Angular Momentum Linear Inverted Pendulum (ALIP) model—which tracks contact angular momentum about the stance foot—they predict the pre-impact state of the next step in closed form given the current state and foot placement. They then formalize conditions that keep this next-step state inside a safe set (preventing leg-crossing, excessive CoM travel, etc.) as a discrete exponential control barrier function (DECBF).

This safety certificate serves a dual purpose: a shaping reward during training that steers RL toward safe behaviors, and a runtime projection filter that minimally adjusts actions to prevent violations. In MuJoCo simulations of the Digit humanoid subjected to periodic lateral disturbances, this method significantly curtailed safety violations compared to standard RL, achieving zero violations when the filter was engaged.
contributions: Derived safety conditions using a discrete exponential control barrier function (DECBF) based on the ALIP step-to-step map, which is affine in foot placement.
Constructed a complementary two-layer framework using the derived safety conditions: training-time reward shaping and execution-time real-time projection filtering.

Demonstrated that three key constraints—lateral leg separation, orbital energy bounds, and CoM reachability—reduce to at most two closed-form 1D intervals under a fixed step period, solvable via simple shortest-distance clipping.
Validated on the Digit bipedal robot in physics simulation, demonstrating dramatic reductions in safety-violation events under demanding periodic lateral disturbances.

sections.heading: Embedding Next-Step Safety Prediction into RL Locomotion
sections.summary: In humanoid locomotion, current foot placement governs stability at the next step, making forward-looking safety design essential. This work merges the interpretable ALIP dynamical model with discrete control barrier functions into an RL framework, certifying safety during both training and execution.
sections.details:
When deploying humanoid robots in cluttered environments, reliability in continuous walking is paramount. Bipedal locomotion is inherently a hybrid dynamical system, featuring discrete switches whenever a swing foot strikes the ground. Consequently, where the robot places its foot right now directly determines whether its state will remain safe throughout the next step.

Historically, reduced-order models such as linear inverted pendulums have excelled at step-to-step prediction and mathematical stability analysis. However, handling varied disturbances and changing gait regimes typically required tedious manual tuning, limiting adaptability. Conversely, modern reinforcement learning (RL) discovers remarkably robust gaits through extensive trial and error in simulation. Yet, lacking an underlying analytical model, RL struggles to offer rigorous mathematical guarantees that the robot will stay within safe limits on the next impact.

This gap motivates the paper. The authors design an RL policy that outputs task-space swing-foot placements, coupled with one-step-ahead predictions from the Angular Momentum Linear Inverted Pendulum (ALIP) model. They apply a discrete exponential control barrier function (DECBF) to derive exact conditions preventing the state from leaving the safe set at the next impact. By using these conditions as training-time reward shaping and as an execution-time projection filter, the framework combines RL's robustness with model-based safety guarantees.

captions.F1: Conceptual overview of the framework on the Digit robot. The policy commands target foot placement and torso pitch. Without safety control (Collision), external disturbances trigger leg crossing and self-collision. Constraining foot placement via ALIP-derived DECBF maintains safe walking (Safe).

sections.heading: Tractable Next-Step Prediction Powered by the ALIP Model
sections.summary: This section details the ALIP formulation, incorporating contact angular momentum to form a step-to-step map. Under a fixed step duration, predictions become affine in foot placement, and orbital energy provides an intuitive metric for identifying leg-crossing risks.
sections.details:
The ALIP model serves as the backbone for predicting gait dynamics. While conventional Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP) models track Center of Mass (CoM) position and velocity, ALIP uses contact angular momentum about the stance foot as an explicit state variable. This enables an accurate, closed-form approximation of the whole-body robot's angular momentum dynamics.

### Step-to-Step Discrete Map
Assuming a constant CoM height $H$ and a fixed step duration $T$, coordinates switch to the new stance foot upon impact. Under the idealized assumption that contact angular momentum is conserved across impact, the transition between steps and the swing-phase continuous evolution can be chained together. The pre-impact state for the next step (sagittal $\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1}^{-}$ and lateral $\boldsymbol{y}_{k+1}^{-}$) can then be expressed in a clean, affine form (linear plus constant terms) with respect to the current state and swing-foot placement $(u_{x,k}, u_{y,k})$.

### Orbital Energy and Leg Crossing
In inverted pendulum dynamics, orbital energy $E$ represents a conserved quantity balancing kinetic and potential energy. In lateral walking, its sign is critical:
- When $E < 0$: The CoM lacks the energy to pass over the stance foot (the apex) and turns back, remaining strictly on one side of the stance foot.
- When $E > 0$: The CoM carries enough energy to pass over the stance foot and cross to the opposite side.

If a lateral push drives the orbital energy positive, the CoM crosses over the stance foot, forcing the robot to cross its legs to avoid falling. For bipedal robots, leg crossing is a primary cause of self-collisions and tripping. The authors enforce an upper bound on this orbital energy to proactively prevent leg-crossing incidents.

captions.F3: Phase plane portraits of orbital energy and designated safe sets. Left: Iso-energy contours. Center: Lateral safe region ($E < 0$ to prevent leg crossing). Right: Sagittal safe region (preventing excessive velocity and CoM overextension).

sections.heading: Double Defense: Training Shaping and Runtime Filtering
sections.summary: The authors construct a discrete exponential control barrier function (DECBF) on top of the ALIP transition map to guarantee forward invariance. This condition is applied at two stages: reward shaping to guide RL exploration, and an analytical projection filter to adjust policy outputs in real time.
sections.details:
The core contribution is how this analytical model integrates into the reinforcement learning loop. The RL policy outputs CoM-relative swing-foot landing targets $(u_{x,k}, u_{y,k})$. With the ALIP step-to-step map, the robot can compute the pre-impact state of the next step instantaneously.

### Discrete Exponential Control Barrier Functions (DECBF)
The safe set is defined as $\mathcal{S} = \{ \boldsymbol{z} \mid B_i(\boldsymbol{z}) \geq 0 \}$. Over a one-step transition, as long as the barrier function's change $\Delta B_i$ satisfies $\Delta B_i + \gamma B_i \geq 0$ for a decay rate $\gamma \in (0, 1)$, the state remains within the safe set indefinitely (forward invariance). The authors introduce an auxiliary margin $s_i$ to quantify this condition as a safety certificate.

### Two-Tier Safety Mechanism
1. **Learning-time Shaping:**
   When the policy proposes a candidate action $u_k$, an exponentially steep penalty $r_{\text{safe}}$ is incurred if the predicted next state violates the safety criterion ($s_i < 0$). This naturally weeds out hazardous landing choices during training, steering policy exploration toward safe regions.
2. **Execution-time Projection Filter:**
   During deployment, if the policy still outputs an unsafe target $u_k^{\text{nom}}$, the runtime filter instantly projects (clips) it to the nearest safe placement satisfying the DECBF conditions before passing it to the whole-body controller.

Traditional Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) are often formulated as continuous-time quadratic programs (QPs) inside the whole-body control loop, which can run into local infeasibilities and high computational overhead. In contrast, this approach operates at the stepping layer, resolving to simple 1D interval clipping that executes reliably and with negligible latency.

sections.heading: Three Core Constraints and Their Fast Geometric Projection
sections.summary: Three physical constraints tailored to bipedal stability—lateral leg separation, lateral orbital energy bounds, and CoM reachability—are formulated as DECBFs. Under a fixed step duration, they reduce to 1D interval checks, enabling closed-form, instantaneous projection.
sections.details:
The authors formalize three barrier functions addressing realistic failure modes in bipedal locomotion:

### 1. Lateral Foot Clearance (Preventing Leg Crossing)
To ensure the swing foot does not collide with or cross the stance leg, a minimum lateral clearance $W_{\min}$ is enforced at impact ($d_{y} \geq W_{\min}$ for right support, $d_{y} \leq -W_{\min}$ for left support). This yields a simple linear inequality in the lateral foot target $u_{y,k}$.

### 2. Orbital Energy Cap (Preventing CoM Crossover)
To stop the CoM from overshooting the stance foot laterally, an upper bound $E_{\max}^{\text{ALIP}} < 0$ is set on the lateral ALIP orbital energy. While quadratic in foot placement, combining it with lateral velocity (angular momentum) forms a well-defined boundary for permissible landing locations.

### 3. CoM Reachability Limits (Preventing Overextension)
Leg length imposes physical boundaries. If the CoM drifts too far from the stance foot at the next impact, the stance leg overextends, inducing a fall. A bounding box $[p_{\min}, p_{\max}]$ (set to $\pm 0.7$ m in experiments) is enforced on sagittal CoM displacement $p_{x,k+1}^{-}$. An upper bound is also placed on sagittal orbital energy to prevent runaway forward speeds.

### Why Can It Be Solved Instantly?
The key insight lies in the implementation geometry. Even though orbital energy expressions look nonlinear, fixing the step time $T$ ensures that, with respect to $u_{x,k}$ and $u_{y,k}$, the feasible set is at most the union of two intervals. Computing the safe placement therefore bypasses numerical QP solvers entirely, boiling down to scalar comparisons and snapping to interval endpoints.

sections.heading: Deployment on Digit: The Hierarchical Control Architecture
sections.summary: This section covers the implementation details for the humanoid Digit in the MuJoCo simulator. A hierarchical architecture pairs an RL high-level policy operating at 33 Hz (commanding swing-foot targets and torso pitch) with a low-level Whole-Body Controller (WBC) running at 1 kHz.
sections.details:
To validate the method, the framework was implemented on Agility Robotics' bipedal robot Digit inside the MuJoCo simulator.

### System Hierarchy and Rates
- **RL Policy (High-Level Planner):** Operates at 33 Hz (30 ms period) with a fixed step duration of $T = 0.35$ s. States are latched at footstrike to compute the target landing position for the upcoming step.
- **Whole-Body Controller (WBC / Low-Level Control):** A QP-based inverse dynamics controller running at 1 kHz. It manages CoM height, rolls and yaws, tracks minimum-jerk swing-foot trajectories, and solves for joint torques subject to friction cones and motor limits. Crucially, **all safety constraints are handled strictly at the RL and filter layer; the WBC contains no safety barrier filters**.

### Observation, Action, and Reward Design
- **Observations:** Inspired by ALIP states, inputs include horizontal CoM positions, running-average velocities, velocity tracking errors, and target velocity commands.
- **Actions:** A 3D vector consisting of CoM-relative horizontal landing coordinates $(u_{x,k}, u_{y,k})$ and target torso pitch $\theta_{\text{pitch}}$. Allowing torso pitch adjustment enables Digit to leverage upper-body inertia to balance.
- **Reward Function:** Comprises terms for velocity tracking, reference foot placement based on walking speed, action smoothness, upright torso posture, and an alignment reward $r_{\text{ALIP}}$ that penalizes discrepancies between Digit's contact angular momentum and the ALIP model. The proposed DECBF-informed policy incorporates the safety shaping penalty $r_{\text{safe}}$ on top of these.

### Training Setup
Policies were trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a 2-layer (256 units each) Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). Episodes terminate early if CoM height deviates outside 0.8 m to 2.0 m (falls or erratic jumps).

sections.heading: Disturbance Experiments: Driving Violations Down to Zero
sections.summary: In walking tests with periodic lateral pushes (0.4 s pulses every 3 s), the unguided baseline suffered frequent leg-crossing and boundary violations. Shaping alone reduced violations by 87%, while combining shaping with the projection filter completely eliminated recorded safety violations.
sections.details:
Policies were evaluated on flat ground while accelerating from 0 to 1.2 m/s under an aggressive disturbance profile: external lateral force pulses applied for 0.4 seconds every 3 seconds.

### Predicting Leg Collisions via Orbital Energy
Visualizing the lateral phase plane ($p_y$ vs. $L_x$) shows that nominal walking stays within the blue region ($E < 0$). Under strong pushes that spike energy into the positive zone (red, $E > 0$), the CoM swings past the stance leg, followed immediately by self-collisions between the limbs. This confirms that tracking orbital energy serves as a dependable indicator of impending collision.

### Comparison Across Four Policy Variants
1. **Baseline (Unconstrained, Filter OFF):** Successfully tracks forward speed, but foot clearance repeatedly drops below the safe margin (0.08 m) at higher speeds, triggering frequent hazardous leg-crossing events.
2. **Baseline + Filter ON:** Post-hoc application of the projection filter reduces violations but fails to prevent them entirely. Because the underlying policy constantly acts near the danger zone, WBC tracking latency still causes the robot to spill over the boundary.
3. **DECBF-Informed (Shaping Only, Filter OFF):** Penalizing unsafe steps during training teaches the robot to adopt a naturally wider, safer stance. The normalized violation metric $\mathcal{M}_\pi$ drops from 1.0 (baseline) down to 0.13—an 87% reduction.
4. **DECBF-Informed + Filter ON (Proposed):** Combining training shaping with runtime projection achieved zero measured safety violations (0.0) across the reported trial.

### Safety vs. Tracking Tradeoff
While the proposed method ensured complete safety, it exhibited longer settling times for lateral velocity transients following major disturbances. To prevent leg crossing, the robot opts for wider protective steps, prioritizing the safety margin over rapid velocity convergence—a classic safety-tracking tradeoff.

captions.F4: Lateral orbital energy phase portrait and leg collisions. Trajectories in the safe region (blue dots, $E < 0$) maintain stability, whereas disturbances pushing trajectories into the red zone ($E > 0$) cause the CoM to overshoot the stance foot, leading to self-collisions.
captions.F5: Velocity tracking (left) and lateral foot clearance at impact (right) under periodic disturbances across four variants: (a) unguided / filter OFF, (b) unguided / filter ON, (c) DECBF-informed / filter OFF, and (d) DECBF-informed / filter ON. The proposed configuration (d) never breaches the 0.08 m safety threshold (dashed line).
captions.F6: Sagittal phase plane trajectories. (a) The unguided policy breaches orbital energy and CoM limits (red and green dashed lines) under disturbance. (b) The DECBF-guided policy stays safely within admissible boundaries.

sections.heading: Summary and Next Steps: Paving the Way for Hardware Deployment
sections.summary: Bridging ALIP step-to-step prediction with discrete control barrier functions substantially boosts safety in RL bipedal locomotion. Future avenues include handling uneven terrain, enabling variable step times, and validating on physical Digit hardware.
sections.details:
This work bridges interpretable reduced-order dynamics (ALIP) and modern reinforcement learning (RL), providing a practical framework that introduces mathematical safety certificates into humanoid locomotion planning. Acting both as training-time guidance (shaping) and runtime intervention (projection filter), the ALIP-based DECBF constraints drastically mitigate the risks of leg-crossing and falls under external pushes.

### Key Takeaway
The primary strength of this formulation is the balance between mathematical rigor and computational lightness. By replacing heavy real-time nonlinear optimization with closed-form scalar interval clipping, the system preserves the responsiveness of the RL policy while adding a dependable safety envelope.

### Limitations and Future Outlook
The authors acknowledge several limitations. Current evaluations assume flat terrain and a fixed step duration ($T = 0.35$ s). In addition, discrepancies between the simplified ALIP template and the full-order dynamics—coupled with low-level tracking lag—mean that template-level guarantees do not automatically translate to absolute full-order safety. Moving forward, the team aims to incorporate multi-layered defenses with continuous CBFs in the whole-body controller, expand to rough-terrain locomotion, and validate the framework on real Digit hardware.

takeaways: Framing the RL action space around task-space foot placement and incorporating ALIP step-to-step prediction injects model-based safety and interpretability into RL locomotion.
Pairing training-time reward shaping with runtime projection filtering provides vastly superior safety compared to applying either mechanism on its own.

Under a fixed step duration, the ALIP model allows lateral clearance, orbital energy limits, and CoM reachability bounds to be solved as closed-form 1D interval clipping, incurring virtually zero computational overhead.
Monitoring the sign of lateral orbital energy enables early detection and prevention of self-collisions (leg-crossing) in bipedal locomotion.
limitations: Template-level guarantees do not guarantee full-order safety due to model mismatches between ALIP and full-order dynamics, as well as tracking errors in the whole-body controller.
The current formulation assumes a fixed step duration ($T = 0.35$ s) on flat ground; extending the framework to variable step timing and uneven terrain remains future work.
Strictly prioritizing leg-crossing prevention results in longer lateral velocity settling times after disturbances, highlighting an inherent safety-versus-tracking tradeoff.
